notes: **Fourteen verbs take être, not avoir.** They're all about moving from place to place or changing state: *aller, venir, arriver, partir, entrer, sortir, monter, descendre, rester, retourner, tomber, naître, mourir, devenir*. The rest — hundreds of them — take *avoir*.

**With être, the past participle agrees with the subject.** *Il est allé*, *elle est all**ée***, *ils sont all**és***, *elles sont all**ées***. The extra letters are silent, but you must write them. This is where the most spelling mistakes happen, even among native speakers.
**All reflexive verbs take être.** *Je me suis levé*, *elle s'est réveillée*, *nous nous sommes amusés*. The pronoun goes **before** the helper verb.

**The negative wraps around the helper verb, and the pronoun goes inside it.** *Je **ne** me suis **pas** levé tôt.* A long chain, but the order is fixed: first part of the negative, pronoun, helper verb, second part of the negative, past participle.
**On est partis** — even though *on* is grammatically singular, the participle is often written plural when it means "we". Native speakers do this all the time, and it's accepted.

**Sortir and monter switch helper verbs when they have an object.** *Je suis sorti* (I went out) versus *j'ai sorti la poubelle* (I took out the trash). There are a few verbs like this; at A1 it's enough to recognize them.
**Au début** = at first. Its cousins: *à la fin* (in the end), *ensuite*, *finalement*.

grammars.title: The fourteen être verbs
body: All about moving or changing state. The easiest way to learn them is in pairs of opposites.
after: *Rentrer* (to go home) and *revenir* (to come back) belong to this group too — they come from *entrer* and *venir*.
⚠️ *Rester* means "to stay", **not** "to rest". To rest is *se reposer*. A common mistake because it looks like the English word.
Other verbs with similar meanings still take *avoir*: *voyager, marcher, courir, visiter*. So don't guess from the meaning — memorize the list.

grammars.title: Matching the ending
body: Exactly the same rule as adjectives in Unit 11: agree with the gender and number of the subject.
after: All these extra letters are **silent**. *Allé*, *allée*, *allés*, *allées* all sound exactly the same: ah-LAY. It's purely a matter of spelling — which is exactly why it's easy to forget.
The sound only changes with participles ending in a consonant: *parti* (pahr-TEE) sounds the same as *partie*, but *mort* (mohr) becomes *morte* (mohrt).

grammars.title: The past of reflexive verbs
body: Always *être*, and the pronoun comes first.

head: se lever
Negative
rows: *ils se sont levés / elles se sont levées*

after: The order is fixed and never changes: **subject pronoun → ne → reflexive pronoun → helper verb → pas → past participle**.
The ones you'll use most: *je me suis réveillé, je me suis couché, je me suis dépêché, on s'est bien amusé, je me suis perdu*.

blocks.text: Real storytelling starts here: putting what has happened next to what will happen, in the same conversation. The table below is your toolkit.

The last two rows are a parting gift: two short patterns that make your French sound far more mature than A1. *Je viens d'arriver* (I've just arrived), *je suis en train de travailler* (I'm busy working).

blocks.title: Phrases to wrap up a long conversation
items: *Ça s'est bien passé ?* — Did it all go well?
*J'ai fait beaucoup de progrès.* — I've made a lot of progress.
*Au début, c'était difficile.* — At first, it was hard.
*Maintenant, ça va mieux.* — Now it's better.
*Je vais continuer.* — I'm going to keep going.
*On se voit bientôt !* — See you soon!
